en: The Buddha Spoke the Sūtra on Listening to the Dharma by the Woman in the Womb,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha together with various bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and upāsakas...
Śreṇika, the upāsikā, and countless devas and people gathered together to listen to the Buddha preach the sūtra.

At that time, there was in the assembly the wife of Kāla, who was sitting with her pregnancy advanced; the child within her womb joined his palms and listened to the sūtra. The Buddha, wishing to let the entire assembly see him, immediately manifested a great radiance that illuminated the wife of Kāla.
All those present in the assembly saw the woman within the womb joining her palms to listen to the sutra, as clearly as if looking into a mirror; there was no difference between them.
The Buddha, employing his eightfold voice, asked the woman within the womb:
"For what reason do you join your palms and listen to the sutra?"
Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, the woman immediately replied to the Buddha:
“Because the people of the world all practice the ten unwholesome deeds, and because I wish to lead them to practice the ten wholesome deeds, I join my palms and listen to the sutra;
furthermore, because the people of the world are consumed by greed, lust, anger, and ignorance, and because the cycle of birth and death does not cease, I join my palms and listen to the sutra.”
"Furthermore, because worldly people are unfilial toward their parents and do not make offerings to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or practitioners of the Way, they join their palms and listen to the sutras.
When the girl had finished speaking these words, she was born;
it was as if a crown prince were born from the right side [of his mother]. The earth shook in six ways, and in the void there were countless devas, and music arose spontaneously.

A rain of various flowers fell, and there appeared natural thousand-petaled lotuses as large as chariot wheels, with stalks made of jewels that resembled blue lapis lazuli; the woman then sat upon a lotus flower.
Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, took a celestial robe and descended from the midst of the sky, saying to the woman:
"Since you are naked, you may take this robe and wear it."
The woman replied, "I do not wear these clothes; are you trying to dress me up?
You are an Arhat and I am a Bodhisattva. You are not of my kind, nor are you of my class; I shall have clothes of my own come to me."
The Buddha said to Kauśika:

"This is not what constitutes the adornment of a bodhisattva. When one has resolved to become a bodhisattva and personally attains the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, only then is one truly adorned as a bodhisattva."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From which country has this woman come?
She should be sent back with her robes."

The Buddha said, "This girl has come from a buddha-field in the southeast; her land is named Pure and is situated one hundred thousand buddha-fields away from here. The girl came from her original land desiring to see the Buddha, and it was natural that someone would bring her this robe."

The garments from her native land then spontaneously appeared in the air with a rustling sound; when the woman saw the garments coming, she put them on and immediately attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and all the people of her native land likewise attained the five supernormal powers.

Once the girl had finished putting on her clothes, she descended from the lotus flower and proceeded to the presence of the Buddha. As soon as she lifted one foot, the earth shook in six ways; she then prostrated herself with her head to the ground to pay homage to the Buddha, saying three times: "Namo Buddhāya!"
Having completed the circumambulation of the Buddha, she knelt down and addressed the Buddha:
"In this assembly there are many women of the Kāla clan; I pray that the Buddha will preach the sutra for them, so that they may obtain male bodies."
The Buddha said:
"I do not cause you to become a man, nor do I cause you to become a woman; all is obtained from one's own bodily actions.
The Buddha said:
“There is one thing by which one may quickly attain manhood.
What is this one thing? It is to resolve to follow the path of a bodhisattva; this is that one thing.

Furthermore, a woman should inwardly observe her own body: it is like a mechanical device where the bones and joints support one another, covered merely by sinews and skin. A woman is always fearful of others, just as owls, crows, snakes, vipers, and frogs do not dare to come out during the day, being constantly afraid of people.”

For example, it is like a maidservant who constantly dwells among foul-smelling impurities; though she may be the daughter of a king, she still fears others. The many evils of women are likewise thus.

At that time, seventy-five women among those seated there, having heard the Buddha preach this sutra, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness. They came forward and prostrated themselves, placing their heads upon the ground to pay homage to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"We vow to give rise to the bodhicitta and become men; we shall not rise until we have attained male bodies."
At that time, seventy-five lay devotees (gṛhapati) came from Śrāvastī to where the Buddha was. Seeing that all the women were before the Buddha, they thought to themselves:
"We have already lost our wives."
He then asked Śāriputra, "These women are all our wives; why are they here? Śāriputra replied:
"If you wish to become a bhikṣuṇī, will you allow us to do so?
The householder replied,
"If you wish to become a bhikṣuṇī, first let us become bhikṣus."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"These seventy-five lay devotees (gṛhapati) all wish to become bhikṣus.
The Buddha called out to them:
"Come, sons of good family; all shall become bhikṣus.
Their hair fell away naturally, the kaṣāya robes were donned upon their bodies, and they held alms bowls in their hands; they all came forward and paid homage to the Buddha.

At that time, seventy-five wives each removed their pearl rings and scattered them all over the Buddha. Immediately, they spontaneously transformed in mid-air into a canopy of seventy-five interlaced pearl necklaces. Within the canopy were couches made of the seven treasures, and upon the couches sat [the Buddha]; by the Buddha’s side, immeasurable bodhisattvas listened to the sutra.

When the seventy-five women saw this miraculous transformation, they were all filled with great joy. By means of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they flew up and stayed in the air. From within the sky, flowers appeared spontaneously and rained down upon the Buddha. Descending from the air, they immediately attained male bodies and came forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"We wish to become bhikṣus."
The Buddha said to Maitreya Bodhisattva,
"Take him away and bestow the precepts.
Maitreya Bodhisattva then bestowed the precepts.
Having become a bhikṣuṇī, she spontaneously possessed seven tiers of transformed flower canopies with stalks like those of lotus flowers. She immediately offered them to her mother and said:

"The Buddha is the teacher who delivers beings above and below heaven; Mother, you should offer these flower canopies to the Buddha, the teacher above and below heaven. After offering the canopies, you too shall become a canopy for the world."
The daughter said to her mother,
"Now I shall resolve upon the mind of a bodhisattva.
Her mother replied to her:

"Since I first conceived you, I have constantly seen the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus in my dreams; I am free from thoughts of greed, anger, and delusion, and my body is at peace. Knowing that the child in my womb is a bodhisattva mahāsattva, this brings me such tranquility."
At that time, having already resolved upon the Bodhisattva mind, her mother obtained a flower parasol and presented it to the Buddha; the earth shook in six ways.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"The number of stars in the four continents may still be known, but the number of parents this girl has liberated throughout her past and present lives cannot be known."
The woman said, "All people call me a woman; I shall now practice with utmost sincerity.
She then transformed herself into the body of an eight-year-old śrāmaṇera.
When the Buddha spoke this sutra and manifested the transformation of the woman, countless people all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, everyone was filled with great joy.
The Sutra on the Woman in the Womb Heard the Dharma Spoken by the Buddha.
